claims.text: A conventional W–Cu composite consists of tungsten powders embedded in a copper matrix.
Tungsten particles can be provided with a uniformly thin, well-bonded WC interfacial coating before composite fabrication.
The WC coating acts as an engineered interphase between tungsten and copper.
The WC interphase mitigates thermal resistance at the W/Cu interface.
The WC interphase serves as a chemical and diffusional barrier.
The WC coating creates a smoother transition between W and Cu.
The WC-mediated transition facilitates electron transport across the W/Cu interface.
The WC-mediated transition facilitates phonon transport across the W/Cu interface.
Facilitating electron and phonon transport reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
WC is robust under mechanical stress.
WC is robust under neutron irradiation.
A thin WC coating will increase the thermal conductivity of W–Cu relative to an otherwise comparable composite made with uncoated tungsten particles.
The WC-coated composite will retain mechanical strength comparable to the uncoated W–Cu control.
The WC-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the uncoated W–Cu control.
The predicted benefits should hold at elevated temperatures and under neutron irradiation representative of fusion-reactor joint and heat-dissipation applications.
The predicted benefits depend on the WC coating being uniformly thin and well bonded.
A coating that is too thick, uneven, or poorly adherent may cause stress concentrations or thermal-expansion mismatch.
Stress concentrations or thermal-expansion mismatch caused by a defective coating may degrade mechanical performance.
A thermal-conductivity improvement greater than 10% is proposed as an example of a statistically significant improvement over the uncoated control.
